---
title: "Overfitting"
description: "A model overfits when it learns training-specific patterns that do not generalize well to new data."
term: "Overfitting"
letter: "O"
category: "Machine Learning"
difficulty: "Beginner"
---

## Simple explanation

Overfitting is like memorizing practice questions instead of learning the
underlying skill. A model performs well on examples it trained on but less
well on new examples.

## Technical explanation

Overfitting occurs when a model captures noise, accidental correlations,
or overly specific details in its training data. A common sign is a widening
gap between training and validation performance, though reliable diagnosis
also depends on representative data and a sound evaluation design.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

A model is useful when it performs on the data it will encounter after
deployment, not merely on its training set. Overfitting can lead to brittle
predictions and misleadingly optimistic training results.

## How it works

As training proceeds, training loss may continue to decrease while
validation loss stops improving or increases. More data, regularization,
early stopping, data augmentation, or a simpler model can help, depending
on the cause. The validation set should guide model selection; a separate
test set should be reserved for final evaluation.

## Practical example

A decision tree grown without limits may memorize individual training
examples. Restricting tree depth or pruning it can improve performance on a
held-out set if the original tree was fitting noise.

## Common misconceptions

- High training accuracy alone is not evidence that a model generalizes.
- Overfitting is not fixed by repeatedly tuning against the test set; doing so leaks test information into model selection.
- Model complexity is one cause, but data leakage, small datasets, and distribution mismatch also affect apparent generalization.
